summary: This workflow reads three monthly case-extract CSV files, stacks them into one dataset, builds several calculated fields (including parsed dates and cleaned text), removes duplicate cases, then summarizes case counts by month and program for a trend report. It scores 6/10, meaning it needs real design decisions rather than a direct line-by-line translation. The main reasons are the Union [5], Formula [6], and Unique [7] tools, which all involve logic that Alteryx and SQL handle differently.

key_components.description: Three monthly CSV files are loaded, one column is renamed, and all three are stacked together into a single dataset using Union [5].
Formula [6] creates several new fields: it parses open dates in multiple formats, flags empty member IDs, and standardizes the status text.
Unique [7] removes duplicate cases by case_id, keeping only the first occurrence of each.
Summarize [9] counts cases by month and program, Sort [10] orders the results by month, and Output Data [11] writes the final trend report.

risks.title: Date parsing logic depends on mixed formats in source data
risks.detail: Formula [6] picks a date format based on separators and string length (e.g. '/' vs length 11), which implies the source open_date column itself has inconsistent formats. Alteryx's date parsing is more forgiving than Redshift's TO_DATE, so each format needs to be tested explicitly or rows may fail or parse incorrectly.

risks.title: Deduplication result depends on row order
risks.detail: Unique [7] keeps the first row per case_id, but 'first' depends on the order rows arrive in Alteryx, which SQL does not guarantee. Without an explicit ORDER BY in a ROW_NUMBER() rewrite, Redshift could keep a different row than Alteryx did, changing results.

risks.title: Union relies on column names, not position
risks.detail: Union [5] is set to match columns by name (ByName), and a column is renamed (program_name to program) in Select [4] right before the union, implying the three input files don't use identical column names. UNION ALL in Redshift matches by position, so columns must be renamed and ordered identically in every SELECT or data will be misaligned.

risks.title: Empty string vs NULL handling may change
risks.detail: Formula [6] treats empty text and NULL the same way for member_id (IsEmpty), but standard SQL distinguishes NULL from an empty string. This needs an explicit check for both cases to avoid missing 'UNKNOWN' labels after migration.

risks.title: Minor function rewrites needed
risks.detail: Formula [6] uses IIF, TitleCase, and date formatting functions that have no direct Redshift equivalent (CASE WHEN, INITCAP, TO_CHAR). These are mechanical rewrites but INITCAP can produce different capitalization results than TitleCase, so output should be spot-checked.

risks.title: CSV inputs have no enforced data types
risks.detail: The three source files are plain CSVs with no built-in column types, so target table types must be defined explicitly when loading with COPY.

next_steps: Document every date format present in the open_date column and write explicit TO_DATE logic for each.
Define an explicit ORDER BY to replicate the 'keep first row' behavior of Unique [7] using ROW_NUMBER().
Align column names and order across all three input sources before writing the UNION ALL that replaces Union [5].
Decide whether member_id should treat empty strings and NULLs the same, and encode that explicitly.
Spot-check INITCAP output against the original TitleCase results for the status field.
Define explicit column data types for the Redshift tables that will receive the COPY-loaded CSV data.
